title: Contentment, not complacency
hookLine: santokh is peace with what is, while still acting

cards: Morning on the bank of the Ravi, and a man walks out with the farmers to work the soil. Tradition says this is Guru Nanak in his later years, at Kartarpur, the town where he settled after his long journeys.
The teacher of the Japji, out plowing. He could have sat and received offerings. Instead, the story goes, he worked the land, and the community ate together from what it grew.
That picture holds today's word in both hands: a deep peace with what is, and a plow still moving.

teach.h: SANTOKH: THE END OF THE RESTLESS MORE.
teach.b: First, the word. Santokh: contentment, enough, the end of the restless more. You've met it often on this path, and a few days ago Asa di Var put it in a chariot: in Satjug, contentment was the chariot.

teach.h: WITHOUT CONTENTMENT, NO ONE IS FULL.
teach.b: In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase: without contentment, no one is satisfied; like dreams, every wish and every effort comes to nothing. Notice the target: not wanting things, but being satisfied.

A person can get everything on the list and still feel hungry, because the list was never the hunger. Third, the trap on the other side. Contentment could slide into complacency: I'm fine, the world's fine, why bother.

teach.h: EARN BY EFFORT, GIVE FROM YOUR HAND.
teach.b: In a salok, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: the one who eats what they earn by their own effort, and gives some of it from their own hand, Nanak, that one recognizes the way. Earn. Give.
Both are verbs. Contentment isn't a couch. Fourth, the field again.
Guru Nanak at Kartarpur, as tradition tells it, is content enough to need no throne, active enough to plow.
So santokh doesn't ask a student to stop studying, a worker to stop asking for a fair wage, or anyone to stop fighting injustice. It asks them to do all that without the gnawing.

teach.h: QUIET THE HUNGER, NOT THE HANDS.

how: Sikhs count santokh, contentment, among the core virtues and pair it with kirat karni, honest work, and vand chhakna, sharing what is earned.

o: peace with enough, while you keep working
settling for less and no longer trying
a fast that ends with a shared meal

games.q: what's inside santokh: tap the pairs.
p: without contentment, no one is satisfied
earn by effort, give from your hand

s: Guru Nanak's salok praises the one who earns by effort and gives from their hand.
Guru Arjan says without contentment no one is satisfied
in the Sukhmani Sahib; every wish and effort, like a dream, comes to nothing.
tradition says Guru Nanak farmed at Kartarpur
the teacher of the hymns, out working the soil.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak at Kartarpur. people would gladly bring offerings and let you sit. what do you do?
o: go out and work the land with the farmers.
leave and travel again so no one can offer anything.
games.why: tradition says he worked the land, and the community ate together from what it grew: content, and still working.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're working toward: a goal, a project, a skill. On the in-breath, say inside: this is enough, right now; on the out-breath: and I'll keep working.
Let both sit side by side, like the farmer's peace and the farmer's plow.

wordCard.voice: Contentment. Santokh: peace with what is, the end of the gnawing for more, held together with honest work and sharing. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: santokh, contentment, one of the virtues the Gurus prize.

carryVoice: Your line: content and working. Peace with what is, and a plow still moving. Go gently.
